title: Labour, Birth & Pain Relief
description: The three stages of labour, types of delivery, and methods of pain relief with their advantages and disadvantages.
content_html:
Signs That Labour Has Begun

Labour is the process by which the baby moves from the uterus into the outside world. It is triggered by hormonal changes that usually occur around 40 weeks of pregnancy. The main signs that labour has started are a show (the discharge of the mucus plug from the cervix), a rupture of the membranes (waters breaking), and the onset of regular, painful contractions that increase in frequency and strength over time.

Not all signs appear together or in the same order. Some women experience their waters breaking before contractions begin; for others, contractions start first. A show may occur up to 72 hours before labour becomes established. Midwives advise timing contractions: once they are occurring every five minutes, lasting around 60 seconds and have continued for at least an hour, it is usually time to contact the maternity unit.

Key Fact

The three main signs of labour are: a show (loss of the mucus plug), rupture of the membranes (waters breaking), and regular, strengthening contractions. All three should be mentioned in exam answers asking for signs of labour.

The Three Stages of Labour

Labour is divided into three distinct stages. The first stage is the longest and involves the cervix gradually dilating to 10 centimetres. This stage can last from a few hours to over 24 hours, particularly in a first labour. It is further divided into the latent phase (0–4 cm, often managed at home) and the active phase (4–10 cm, usually in hospital). Contractions become longer, stronger and closer together as the cervix opens fully.

The second stage begins when the cervix is fully dilated and ends with the birth of the baby. The mother actively pushes with each contraction to move the baby down the birth canal. This stage typically lasts from minutes up to about two hours. The baby's head usually appears first, a moment called crowning. The third stage involves delivery of the placenta, usually within 30 minutes of the birth; it may be managed actively (an injection of oxytocin speeds placental separation) or allowed to happen naturally.

A natural (vaginal) birth is where the baby is born through the birth canal without surgical intervention. If labour stalls or the baby shows signs of distress, an assisted delivery may be needed. Forceps are smooth metal instruments shaped like large spoons that are placed around the baby's head to guide it out during a contraction; they may leave temporary marks on the baby's face. A ventouse (vacuum extraction) uses a soft cup attached to the baby's head by suction to help guide the baby out; it is less likely to cause maternal tearing but may leave a temporary swelling on the baby's head called a chignon.

A caesarean section (C-section) is a surgical operation in which the baby is delivered through an incision in the mother's abdomen and uterus. It may be planned in advance (elective) if there is a known risk, such as placenta praevia or a breech presentation, or performed as an emergency if complications arise during labour. Recovery from a caesarean takes longer than from a vaginal birth, and the mother will usually remain in hospital for two to three days. Around one in four babies born in the UK is delivered by caesarean section.

Methods of Pain Relief

Pain relief in labour ranges from simple natural methods to medical interventions. gas and air (Entonox) is the most widely used form of pain relief in UK maternity units. It is inhaled through a mouthpiece at the start of each contraction and takes effect within seconds. Advantages include that it is self-administered, does not slow labour and wears off quickly; disadvantages are that it may cause dizziness or nausea and only takes the edge off pain rather than eliminating it.

Pethidine is an opioid drug given by injection into the thigh or buttock. It takes 20 minutes to work and lasts three to four hours. Advantages include that it allows the mother to rest between contractions; disadvantages are that it can cross the placenta and cause drowsiness and breathing difficulties in the newborn, and it may cause nausea in the mother. An epidural involves an anaesthetist inserting a fine tube into the epidural space in the lower back; drugs (usually a mix of local anaesthetic and opioid) are delivered continuously or on demand. An epidural provides the most effective pain relief but can slow labour, limit mobility, increase the likelihood of an assisted delivery and cause a drop in blood pressure. A TENS (Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation) machine uses small electrical pulses delivered via pads on the back to interrupt pain signals; it is safe, drug-free and controlled by the mother, but is most effective only in early labour.

Key Fact

Natural methods of pain relief include water (a birthing pool can soothe pain and allow mobility), breathing and relaxation techniques, massage, and hypnobirthing. These carry no medical risk to mother or baby and can be used alongside other methods; however, they may not be sufficient for more intense labour pain.

Students often muddle forceps and ventouse. Remember: forceps are metal instruments that cup around the head (think of large salad servers), while a ventouse uses suction. A ventouse is less likely to tear the perineum but cannot be used if the baby is very premature or in certain positions. Forceps require a larger episiotomy but can rotate the baby's head if it is in the wrong position. In the exam, name the method correctly and state one specific feature — do not describe them interchangeably.
exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to 'describe' a method of pain relief, you must include what it is, how it works, and at least one advantage and one disadvantage to access full marks. Simply naming the method scores only 1 mark. For 'evaluate' questions on types of delivery, consider both the benefits (e.g. planned timing of a caesarean) and the drawbacks (e.g. longer recovery, increased infection risk) and reach a supported conclusion.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Labour has three stages: the first (cervix dilates to 10 cm), the second (birth of the baby) and the third (delivery of the placenta); the three main signs it has begun are a show, rupture of the membranes, and regular contractions.
  • Delivery may be natural (vaginal), assisted (forceps or ventouse) or surgical (caesarean section), each with distinct indications and implications for mother and baby.
  • Pain relief options range from self-administered gas and air and TENS through to epidural anaesthesia; each carries advantages and disadvantages that must be weighed against the individual mother's circumstances.

glossary_terms.definition: The discharge of the mucus plug from the cervix, signalling that the cervix is beginning to soften and dilate in preparation for labour.
The stage during which the cervix dilates from closed to fully open (10 centimetres), allowing the baby's head to pass through.
A 50:50 mixture of oxygen and nitrous oxide inhaled through a mouthpiece to reduce pain perception during contractions.
A surgical operation in which the baby is delivered through an incision in the mother's abdomen and uterus, either planned or as an emergency.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a sign that labour has begun?
A) The baby drops lower in the pelvis at 36 weeks
B) Braxton Hicks contractions begin
C) The mucus plug is discharged from the cervix (a show)
D) The mother experiences heartburn
practice_questions.marks: C) The mucus plug is discharged from the cervix (a show) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two types of assisted delivery that a midwife or obstetrician may use if labour is not progressing.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for: forceps delivery [1]; ventouse (vacuum extraction) [1]. (Caesarean section is a surgical delivery, not an assisted vaginal delivery — do not credit as a third option here.) [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one disadvantage of using an epidural as a method of pain relief during labour.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying a disadvantage (e.g. 'an epidural can slow labour'). A second mark for development (e.g. 'this is because the reduced sensation makes it harder for the mother to push effectively during the second stage'). A third mark for a further development or linked consequence (e.g. 'which increases the likelihood of needing an assisted delivery using forceps or ventouse, adding further risk of tearing or bruising'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the second stage of labour. Give one example of what the midwife might do to support the mother during this stage.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): the second stage begins when the cervix is fully dilated at 10 centimetres and ends with the birth of the baby; the mother actively pushes the baby down through the birth canal during contractions (2 marks for a clear description of start, process and end; 1 mark for a partial answer).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, the midwife may coach the mother's breathing and pushing technique, monitor the baby's heart rate using a Doppler or CTG monitor, and prepare for crowning by asking the mother to stop pushing briefly to allow a controlled delivery of the head (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague answer). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Amina is 38 weeks pregnant and discussing her birth plan with her midwife. She is anxious about pain and wants to avoid medication that could affect her baby.

Discuss the pain relief options that would be most appropriate for Amina to consider.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion identifying at least two appropriate options (e.g. TENS — drug-free, safe, self-controlled, but limited to early labour; water/birthing pool — reduces pain and aids mobility, no drug transfer to baby; breathing and relaxation techniques — no risk, widely available, but may be insufficient for intense pain), explaining why each fits Amina's concern, and acknowledging a counter-argument (e.g. if pain becomes severe, she may need to reconsider; gas and air has minimal impact on the baby and could be a middle-ground option). A conclusion is reached that reflects Amina's stated priorities.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two relevant options identified and explained with some reference to Amina's situation.
Developing (2 marks): One option identified with brief explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A first-time mother is considering whether to include a caesarean section in her birth plan as her preferred method of delivery.

Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of a planned (elective) caesarean section compared with a natural vaginal birth.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation covering clear advantages of an elective caesarean (predictable timing, avoids prolonged labour, reduces risk of perineal trauma, preferred in certain medical conditions such as placenta praevia) and significant disadvantages (major surgery with longer recovery of 6–8 weeks, increased risk of infection and blood clots, baby misses beneficial exposure to vaginal bacteria, may affect breastfeeding establishment, future pregnancies carry scar tissue risks). The vaginal birth alternative is weighed (lower complication risk long-term, faster recovery, better breastfeeding outcomes) against its own uncertainties (unpredictable duration, potential for tearing, possibility of an emergency caesarean anyway). A substantiated judgement is reached — for example, that an elective caesarean is justified when there is a medical indication but is not recommended as a preference for convenience alone. Judgement must be supported with reasoning.
Secure (5–6 marks): At least two developed points on each side with an attempt at a conclusion.
Developing (3–4 marks): Points identified but largely one-sided or without a clear judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic, undeveloped points. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following correctly describes what happens during the first stage of labour?
options: The mother pushes the baby out through the birth canal
The cervix dilates from closed to fully open at 10 centimetres
The waters break and labour ends

knowledge_checks.q: Which method of pain relief in labour works by delivering small electrical pulses to the lower back through adhesive pads?
A ventouse delivery uses _____ applied to the baby's head to assist birth.
Pethidine is described as a disadvantage for the baby because it can cross the _____ and cause breathing difficulties in the newborn.
Match each method of pain relief to its key feature.
right: Most effective in early labour only; drug-free
Most effective pain relief; can slow labour and limit mobility

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three main signs that labour has begun?
flashcard_questions.a: A show, rupture of the membranes (waters breaking), and regular strengthening contractions.
The discharge of the mucus plug from the cervix as it begins to soften and dilate.

flashcard_questions.q: To what measurement must the cervix dilate before the second stage of labour begins?
What happens during the third stage of labour?
flashcard_questions.a: The placenta is delivered, usually within 30 minutes of the baby's birth.
An assisted birth using a suction cup attached to the baby's head to guide it out.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one advantage and one disadvantage of gas and air.
flashcard_questions.a: Advantage: self-administered and wears off quickly. Disadvantage: only reduces, not eliminates, pain.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is pethidine considered a risk for the baby?
flashcard_questions.a: It can cross the placenta and cause drowsiness and breathing difficulties in the newborn.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one advantage of an epidural as pain relief in labour.
flashcard_questions.a: It provides the most effective pain relief available during labour.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one disadvantage of an epidural.
flashcard_questions.a: It can slow labour and increase the likelihood of an assisted delivery.
A surgical operation delivering the baby through an incision in the abdomen and uterus.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two natural methods of pain relief that carry no drug risk to the baby.
flashcard_questions.a: Water (birthing pool) and breathing or relaxation techniques.

hero_image_caption: Labour and birth bring together medical support and personal choice as a new life enters the world.
